newsitem.title: USA: Calif. researchers identify breast cancer gene.
newsitem.headline: Calif. researchers identify breast cancer gene.

text.p: Researchers said on Friday that they have identified what may be a key gene involved in breast cancer.

Scientists at California's Stanford University believe the gene, called tumour susceptibility gene 101 or TSG101, suppresses tumours when present, but when missing or defective it may increase the likelihood of cancer.

TSG101 is the first gene identified through an innovative strategy called random homozygous knockout, devised by Stanford genetics professor Stanley Cohen and postdoctoral fellow Limin Li. Their research is reported in the latest issue of the journal Cell.

Cohen and Stanford colleagues looked at tissue from women with late-stage breast cancer and found that a piece of the TSG101 gene was missing in seven out of 15 cancers, whereas the gene was intact in neighbouring, healthy breast tissue from the same patients.

Scientists have previously discovered two genes, BRCA1 and BRCA2, that are altered in a high percentage of women with relatively rare, inherited forms of breast cancer, but are normal in most breast cancers.

But the newly identified gene was found to be defective in breast cancers that were not necessarily inherited, Stanford University said. "This is significant because, overall, the vast majority of breast cancers arise through spontaneous mutations rather than through inheritance," it said.
The researchers said more extensive research was needed to get more accurate information about the frequency of TSG101 defects in breast cancer.

Using Cohen and Li's method, scientists can simultaneously "knock out" both copies of a gene in a cell without knowing the gene's identity or function. Then they look among millions of these mutant cells for individual cells that are capable of forming cancers.
By identifying the gene disactivated in the cancer-forming cells, researchers can isolate genes called tumour suppressors, which normally are necessary to stop cancer development.
"It is an elegant method because you can get directly to the gene," said Uta Francke, a Stanford genetics professor working with Li and Cohen.
